paper_title: AuXSpec: Learning to Autoformalize Program Specifications via Executable Postconditions

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Formal specifications define intended program behavior and underpin verification, but writing them in theorem provers such as Lean is slow and expertise-intensive, making specification a major bottleneck to scaling formally correct code. Autoformalization from natural-language problems is promising, yet training specification models requires scalable feedback on whether generated specifications capture intended behavior. Prior approaches obtain this feedback through explicit proofs or separately implemented code with formal correspondence proofs, both expensive. We introduce AuXSpec, a Lean framework that pairs declarative postconditions with executable counterparts, obtained through type class resolution when possible and otherwise defined separately with an equivalence proof. Test cases can then evaluate declarative specifications by execution, letting us use agreement as a reinforcement-learning reward. Using AuXSpec, we synthesize 3,037 LeetCode problems and expand training to 19.5K samples through expert iteration on Codeforces. Experiments show that training Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.8-27B with the execution-based reward improves SpecGen pass@4 on AuXSpec-Test 0.7% $\to$ 82.7% and 14.3% $\to$ 84.3%, and the 27B model outperforms all frontier models. On the out-of-domain Verina benchmark with its original prompts, both models improve 7.0% $\to$ 90.5% and 21.9% $\to$ 90.5% and surpass VeriSpecGen-30B-A3B, the prior state of the art among open-source specification models, on pass@1 (theirs 47.6% vs. ours 73.7% and 84.5%) and pass@4 (theirs 63.9% at pass@10 vs. ours 90.5%). We release the weights of the trained 9B and 27B models and the 3,037 problems with test cases, including the 300-problem AuXSpec-Test benchmark with expert review and correctness proofs for future evaluation. Models and data: https://huggingface.co/collections/eth-algopt/auxspec. Website: https://auxspec.org

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Formal program specifications define the correct behavior of program over all valid inputs, providing the reference against which implementations can be proved correct or tested. Yet writing such specifications in an interactive theorem prover requires substantial expertise and effort, making specification fundamental barrier to scaling formal code verification and generation. As AI models make rapid progress in generating code and proving its correctness, this barrier becomes increasingly important: realizing the promise of formally correct code requires automating specification itself. Autoformalization from natural-language programming problems offers path forward, but immediately raises central question: when does generated formal specification faithfully capture the intended problem? This question is particularly important in modern code-generation pipelines. Large language models (LLMs) can generate solutions to programming problems (e.g., LeetCode) from natural-language descriptions. These solutions can be evaluated using input-output test cases, which provide scalable *Equal contribution. Corresponding author: kyng@inf.ethz.ch.

However, passing test cases does not guarantee correctness, as solution may still fail on untested inputs (Shi et al., 2026). Formal verification offers stronger guarantee. Given specification, which consists of precondition defining valid inputs and postcondition characterizing correct outputs (Endres et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2026), theorem prover like Lean can formally prove that an implementation satisfies its specification for every valid input. This guarantee depends on the specification correctly capturing the natural-language problem, yet producing such specifications at scale remains difficult. Manually curating specifications requires substantial expert effort: Clever and Verina contain only 161 and 189 problems, respectively (Thakur et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2026a). Automated methods can scale further, but may produce incorrect specifications (Dougherty & Mehta, 2025; Bursuc et al., 2026; Dougherty et al., 2026). Scaling specification therefore requires more than generating formal statements. It also requires efficient and scalable feedback on whether generated specifications match the source problem, analogous to the test-case feedback used to train code-generation models. Training specification generators has been explored in auto-active verification languages, where verifier, like an SMT solver, provides the reward by checking candidate specifications on test cases (Yan et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026; Baksys et al., 2025). However, SMT solvers limit the complexity of specifications that can be checked (Yang et al., 2026; Ye et al., 2026a), motivating the use of interactive theorem provers such as Lean. In Lean, prior work checks generated specifications by turning each test case into theorem to be proved, method known as symbolic specification testing (Lahiri, 2024; Ye et al., 2026b; Yang et al., 2026). These theorems can require nontrivial proofs, especially when the specification involves unbounded quantifiers. If proof cannot be found, the test case may be left unresolved or evaluated by an LLM judge. Thus, unlike in code generation (Wang et al., 2025; He et al., 2026), test cases do not directly provide cheap rewards for training specification generators in Lean  (Table 1)  . To address this issue, we propose AUXSPEC, framework for training models to generate program specifications in Lean 4. AUXSPEC retains declarative postcondition that specifies correctness independently of the implementation and pairs it with an executable postcondition for evaluating test cases, pairing with long history in formal methods (Section 6). For each synthesized problem, we prove postcondition equivalence theorem, separately from generation (Section 2), showing that the two postconditions agree for every valid input. This theorem allows us to evaluate any number of test cases by direct execution in Lean, without proving each case separately. We build synthesis pipeline to generate Lean specifications and implementations for 3,037 LeetCode problems. For model training, we combine synthesized data from LeetCode and Codeforces with expert iteration to obtain 19.5K samples for supervised fine-tuning (SFT). We fine-tune Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.8-27B on these samples and then apply reinforcement learning (RL) with our execution-based reward on 13,637 tasks over 8,579 further problems. The resulting AUXSPEC-9B and AUXSPEC-27B models can generate and repair both specifications and implementations. Relative to its base model, AUXSPEC-27B improves SpecGen pass@4 from 14.3% to 84.3% on AUXSPEC-Test and from 21.9% to 90.5% on Verina with its original prompts. The corresponding improvements for AUXSPEC-9B are from 0.7% to 82.7% and from 7.0% to 90.5%. Moreover, RL with our execution-based reward improves SpecGen pass@4 over SFT alone for both model sizes (Section 5.4).

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Our contributions are threefold. Executable specification format. We introduce specification format that pairs declarative postcondition with an executable Boolean postcondition, obtained through type class resolution in Lean when decidability instance exists and defined separately otherwise. postcondition equivalence theorem proves that the two agree on valid inputs (Section 2). AUXSPEC dataset and AUXSPEC-Test. We release the 3,037 LeetCode problems with specifications, implementations, frozen test cases and postcondition equivalence proofs, including AUXSPEC-Test, an expert-reviewed subset of 300 problems that serves as benchmark for Lean specification generation (Sections 3 and 3.3). AUXSPEC-9B-RL and AUXSPEC-27B-RL. Using our execution-based reward, we train and release open-weight models that generate and repair Lean specifications and implementations from natural-language descriptions. AUXSPEC-27B-RL surpasses all frontier models in domain, and both models surpass the prior state of the art among open-source specification models on Verina (Tables 4 and 5).

sections.title: 2 PROBLEM FORMULATION
sections.content: In our autoformalization setup, we represent each programming problem with Lean file. This section describes the file format, the generation and repair tasks over its components, and the acceptance criteria used in data synthesis, model training and evaluation. Format. For each programming problem, we take natural-language problem description, input constraints, and test cases as input, and aim to produce Lean file containing specification, an implementation, two theorem statements, and executable tests (Figures 13 and 14 in Appendix G.2.1). The specification consists of precondition defining valid inputs, declarative postcondition characterizing correct outputs independently of how they are computed, and an executable postcondition that expresses the same condition in form that can be directly evaluated on test cases by Lean. The implementation is an algorithm that computes an output from given input. The file also contains two theorems: the postcondition equivalence theorem, asserting that the two postconditions agree on valid inputs, and the correctness theorem, asserting that the implementation satisfies the declarative postcondition. We include the test cases in the Lean file as #guard commands that check the precondition, the executable postcondition and the implementation. We illustrate the format with two synthesized problems, Count Number of Special Subsequences and Continuous Subarray Sum (Appendix G.2.1). Tasks. We train our models on specification generation (SpecGen) and code generation (CodeGen), as in prior work (Ye et al., 2026a), and their repair variants, SpecGen-Repair and CodeGen-Repair  (Table 2)  . The synthesis pipeline performs these tasks and assembles the generated components into complete Lean files to build the training data and test set. Table 2. Input and output of each task. Broken is the rejected output that repair task revises, and Diagnostics are the compiler errors and failed test cases of that output. Test layers check the output (Table 7 in Appendix A.2).

Proofs. The Lean file includes two theorem statements, whose proofs are left as sorry throughout data synthesis, training, and evaluation. We instead adopt executable tests and LLM judges as acceptance criteria, and assess the reliability of these checks separately. For 35.5% of the synthesized problems, the executable postcondition is obtained directly through decidability instances and agrees with the declarative postcondition by construction. After synthesis, we attempt to prove postcondition equivalence for all 3,037 problems, and 99.0% are provable without modifying their definitions (Section 3.2), which indicates that the proofs expose errors beyond tests and judges in only 1.0% of the synthesized problems. Semantic agreement with the problem therefore rests on the test cases, the judges and expert review (Section 3.3). We do not require correctness proofs for generated implementations either, since such proofs are long (a median of about 160 lines on AUXSPEC-Test, Appendix H.3) and implementation verification is not the focus of this work. We nevertheless prove correctness for all 300 AUXSPEC-Test problems to provide verified references for evaluation (Section 3.3).

sections.title: 3 DATA SYNTHESIS
sections.content: To train and evaluate models on the tasks defined in Section 2, we synthesize and release 3,037 LeetCode problems in our Lean format. The dataset provides training data and includes held-out, expert-reviewed set of 300 problems, AUXSPEC-Test, for evaluation. In this section, we describe the synthesis pipeline, report its results and introduce AUXSPEC-Test.

sections.title: 3.1 SYNTHESIS PIPELINE
sections.content: Our pipeline takes problem description and test cases as input (Figure 1). We first make problemlevel plan, then generate the declarative specification (the precondition and the declarative postcondition), the executable postcondition, and the implementation in three stages. In each stage, we plan and generate component, validate it against the acceptance criteria of Section 2 and repair it if validation fails. We separate the stages to prevent the generation of later component from overfitting the test cases or weakening an accepted specification (Baksys et al., 2025). Finally, we assemble the accepted components into Lean file in the format of Section 2. Inputs. We collect 3,109 LeetCode problems (Xia et al., 2025) with typed function signatures, reference solutions, and existing test cases  (Table 3)  . Before synthesis, we construct and freeze positive and negative test cases for each problem (Appendix G.1.1). positive test case pairs valid input with the output of the reference solution, which is computed independently of the specifications under synthesis (Wang et al., 2025; Fu et al., 2025; He et al., 2026). negative test case is either an invalid input or valid input paired with an incorrect output. sections.title: 3.2 RESULTS
sections.content: The pipeline synthesizes 3,037 of the 3,109 problems (97.7%, Appendix G.5). Only 34.8% of the problems pass all stages at the first attempt, and repair recovers most of the others within 2 rounds (Appendix G.4.1). For 35.5% of the synthesized problems, the declarative postcondition can be made executable by decide. These executable postconditions pass validation on the first attempt in 98.1% of cases, compared with 52.4% for those generated separately (Appendix G.2.2). Since tests on small inputs do not detect nontermination or inefficiency, the implementation judge rejects 19.6% of the generated implementations that pass all test cases (Appendix G.3.1). After synthesis, we attempt to prove the postcondition equivalence theorem for all 3,037 problems (Appendix H), and the attempts expose statement errors in 31 problems (1.0%), all of which had passed the test layers and the judges. Most of these errors (19) are in the declarative postcondition, which execution never evaluates (Table 39 in Appendix H). We repair the 31 problems and then prove the theorem. For the remaining 99.0% of the problems, the theorem is provable as synthesized.

sections.title: 3.3 AUXSPEC-TEST
sections.content: AUXSPEC-Test is held-out evaluation benchmark consisting of 300 problems from the synthesized dataset, with 72 easy, 155 medium and 73 hard problems, yielding 834 samples across four tasks (Table 11 in Appendix C.3). We manually review every component against the problem description and identify errors in 21 problems (Appendix I.1). Attempts to prove the correctness theorems reveal one additional error (Appendix H.3). We correct these 22 problems and prove correctness for all 300; the remaining 278 problems (92.7%) require no changes to their definitions. These reviewed problems serve as references for evaluating model-generated specifications and implementations. For SpecGen, we pair generated specification with the reference implementation, and for CodeGen, generated implementation with the reference specification. sections.title: 4.1 TRAINING DATA
sections.content: Each synthesized problem contributes samples to the tasks of Section 2. The generation tasks take accepted components as targets, and the repair tasks take components rejected during synthesis as inputs. To obtain starting point for RL that reasons concisely, we rephrase the long and often redundant reasoning recorded during synthesis into short trace of the planning behind generated component or the diagnosis behind repair (Appendix G.6). Increasing the number of problems improves SpecGen performance more than continued pretraining on Mathlib corpus (Appendix E.2). We therefore source further problems for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL) from Codeforces, AtCoder, Aizu, CodeChef and GeeksforGeeks through TACO (Li et al., 2023) and open-r1/codeforces (Penedo et al., 2025)  (Table 3)  . To eliminate the risk of data contamination, the final SFT and RL data are disjoint from each other and from the evaluation benchmarks (Appendix C).

sections.title: 4.2 SUPERVISED FINE-TUNING
sections.content: We expand the SFT data to 19.5K training samples over 3 rounds of expert iteration (Polu et al., 2023), each fine-tuning Qwen3.8-27B from the base model on the accumulated samples and adding the outputs that meet the acceptance criteria of Section 2. SpecGen performance rises as the data grow, with no sign of saturation (Appendix E.1). Fine-tuning Qwen3.5-9B (Qwen Team, 2026a) and Qwen3.8-27B (Qwen Team, 2026b) on these samples yields AUXSPEC-9B-SFT and AUXSPEC27B-SFT, with the settings of Appendix B.

sections.title: 4.3 REINFORCEMENT LEARNING
sections.content: We further apply RL to the SFT models for 1 epoch on 13,637 SpecGen and CodeGen tasks over 8,579 problems disjoint from the SFT data and AUXSPEC-Test  (Table 3)  , yielding AUXSPEC-9BRL and AUXSPEC-27B-RL. We ablate the components of our recipe (Appendix F.2) and compare with VeriSpecGen on the same backbone (Appendix F.1). Reward design. Since the SFT models solve only 10.1% and 18.7% of SpecGen problems at pass@1 (Section 5.2), binary reward that requires all acceptance criteria induces low reward variance, which slows optimization even when the reward is faithful to the acceptance criteria (Razin et al., 2025). We therefore score each rollout with 6-stage progressive reward that follows the order of the acceptance criteria of Section 2 (Le et al., 2022; Huang et al., 2026). Failing stage assigns the rollout the value of that stage, from format (0), compilation (0.1), test execution (0.2), test case alignment (0.1), non-tautology (0.1) to overall quality (0.4), and passing all stages yields 1. With vk the value of stage k, the reward of rollout is r(y) = (cid:26)1 vk if passes all stages, if is the first stage that fails. (1) We value non-tautology at 0.1 to rank specifications that restate the computation without specifying the problem below failed tests. Replaying the training rollouts shows that at this value tautological specifications have negative mean advantage in every group, whereas at higher value such as 0.3 the advantage turns positive in groups where no rollout passes (Appendix E.3.2). Two kinds of rollouts that pass all stages receive partial credit instead of 1, enumerative specifications (0.4) and slow implementations (0.5), which evaluation accepts. To prevent reward hacking, test counts toward the required number of tests only if it calls declaration of the output, which excludes tests that hold trivially. Falling short of this number reduces the reward to 0.1. Hard-coding answers, by special-casing the test inputs or by copying the given test cases into the implementation, sets the reward to 0, and so does returning repair unchanged (Appendix E.3.1). Self-repair. Besides generation, we train on repair tasks built from failed rollouts of the current policy, which avoids distribution shift (Kumar et al., 2025). sections.title: 5.1 SETUP
sections.content: Training settings, including hyperparameters and the Lean environment, are listed in Appendix B, and the sampling settings in Appendix B.2. We report pass@k for {1, 4}, the fraction of problems with at least one of samples meeting the acceptance criteria of Section 2 (Appendix D.1). All evaluated models receive the same prompts (Appendix K). The baselines are our backbones, frontier models and prior work on specification generation. Instruct Models: To isolate the effect of fine-tuning, we evaluate the backbones Qwen3.5-9B (Qwen Team, 2026a) and Qwen3.8-27B (Qwen Team, 2026b). Frontier Models: Claude-Opus-5 (Anthropic, 2026a), Claude-Sonnet-5 (Anthropic, 2026b), GPT-5.6-Sol and GPT-5.6-Luna (OpenAI, 2026), Kimi-K3 (Kimi Team, 2026), and DeepSeekV4-Pro and DeepSeek-V4-Flash (DeepSeek-AI, 2026). Prior Work: We compare against VeriSpecGen (Ye et al., 2026b), which fine-tunes Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B on refinement trajectories distilled from closed teacher, using the reported results as the models are not publicly available.

sections.title: 5.2 MAIN RESULTS
sections.content: We report the performance on the in-domain test set in Table 4. Training improves SpecGen pass@4 from 0.7% to 82.7% for the 9B backbone and from 14.3% to 84.3% for the 27B backbone. AUXSPEC-27B-RL surpasses every frontier model in both pass@1 and pass@4 on SpecGen and CodeGen, with 65.7% SpecGen pass@1 (vs. 57.7% for Claude-Opus-5, the strongest frontier model). The 9B RL model also outperforms every frontier model in SpecGen pass@1 (58.6%). On the repair tasks, the 27B RL model attains the best CodeGen-Repair pass@1 (88.1%) and stays within 2 points of the best result on the other metrics, while the 9B RL model surpasses most frontier models in SpecGen-Repair pass@1. To assess false positives of SpecGen acceptance, we prove the postcondition equivalence theorem for 99.2% of accepted RL outputs (Appendix H.4), and expert review confirms 90 of 100 sampled outputs, with all errors in the validity predicate (Appendix I.2).

sections.title: 5.4 RL ANALYSIS
sections.content: Reinforcement learning from the SFT models improves SpecGen pass@1 on AUXSPEC-Test from 10.1% to 58.6% for the 9B model and from 18.7% to 65.7% for the 27B model (Table 4 and Figure 2a), and the gains transfer to Verina, where SpecGen pass@1 rises from 37.3% to 87.0% and from 57.3% to 91.9% (Table 5 and Figure 2b). The reward is computed on the synthesized problems only, yet Verina scores each specification against the reference specification on test cases absent from the prompt, so the policy learns faithfulness to the description beyond the frozen test cases. Gains at pass@1 can also come from sharpening the sampling distribution, in which case the SFT model would catch up at large (Yue et al., 2025). SpecGen pass@256 of AUXSPEC-27B-SFT (85.7%) stays below pass@8 of AUXSPEC-27B-RL (88.2%), and the SFT model therefore needs more than 32 times the samples of the RL model to reach this pass rate. Within 256 samples, 33 of the 300 problems are solved only by the RL model and 1 only by the SFT model (Appendix E.3.3). The RL model is also token-efficient, requiring 20.3% of the output tokens per solved SpecGen sample of the most economical frontier model (Appendix D.2). We utilize progressive reward to assign fine-grained credit to partial progress. binary reward assigns 0 to every rollout that fails any stage and provides no signal in groups where no sample passes. With fine-grained values, the group-relative advantage can distinguish better samples from worse ones within group, which raises the probability of the better samples until the group saturates. Replaying the rollouts of the final runs confirms the denser signal. Groups without passing rollout make up 37% of SpecGen groups for the 27B model and 47% for the 9B model and would be discarded by dynamic sampling under binary reward (Yu et al., 2025), whereas the progressive reward yields nonzero variance in 87.9% and 86.2% of them (Appendix E.3.1). The rollouts shift accordingly and follow this group-relative credit. In the early stage, few CodeGen groups contain fast and correct program, where slow but correct programs receive positive advantage and grow (up to 67.4% of correct CodeGen rollouts of the 27B model). These slow programs then decrease gradually as fast programs appear (0.4% at the end), whereas the 9B model, which solves fewer CodeGen problems, ends with more of them (30.4%). Enumerative specifications show similar pattern (17.0% to 2.8% of otherwise accepted specifications for the 27B model, Figure 2c). The selection of the intermediate values relies on the reward dynamics, which we measure by replaying the training rollouts and recording the advantage of each stage in groups of different strength.

sections.title: 6 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Specification generation. Specification autoformalization translates requirements into formal specifications. Prior work studies postcondition generation from natural language (Endres et al., 2024), executable Python specifications (Chen et al., 2026) and user intent in Dafny (Lahiri, 2024). Training for specification generation. Training for program specification generation has concentrated on auto-active verification languages (Section 1). In Lean and Rocq, prior work checks specification by proving each test case separately or by searching for counterexamples (Feng et al., 2026), and reinforcement learning from verifier feedback has targeted correctness proofs (Li et al., 2026b) but remains underexplored for specification generation (Baksys et al., 2025). Specification generators there are trained instead on synthesized and repaired examples, where reference implementation labels tests, proof attempt checks each labeled test, and LLM judgments guide refinement when proof automation is inconclusive (Ye et al., 2026b). AUXSPEC also labels tests with reference solutions, and relies on the test results of the executable postcondition to filter the training data and to define the reinforcement-learning reward (Section 2). Executable specifications. The executability of specifications has long been debated in formal methods. Executable specifications can be validated against intended behavior by execution (Kemmerer, 1985; Fuchs, 1992), whereas declarative specifications are more expressive and independent of any algorithm (Hayes & Jones, 1989). Runtime assertion checking and property-based testing run contracts and properties as tests (Meyer, 1992; Cheon & Leavens, 2002; Claessen & Hughes, 2000), and proof assistants test conjectures before proving them (Berghofer & Nipkow, 2004; Lean Community, 2024). Boolean reflection pairs proposition with Boolean function and proof that the two agree (Gonthier & Mahboubi, 2010; Paraskevopoulou et al., 2015). Executable counterparts can also be derived automatically from inductive relations in proof assistants, but the derivation covers restricted class of relations, and users still write executable variants by hand and prove that the two agree (Berghofer et al., 2009; Paraskevopoulou et al., 2022). AUXSPEC utilizes both sides of this trade-off, where we let models generate the executable variants, step that previously required manual curation. Adjacent settings. Generating specifications for existing implementations utilizes verifier to check the specification against the code but assumes the code is correct (Chen et al., 2025; Yan et al., 2026). In this setting, reinforcement learning has included executable checks on mutated-output tests in the reward (Huang et al., 2026). Our SpecGen task instead starts from the problem description, input constraints and tests, without access to an implementation. Vericoding benchmarks evaluate the reverse task, generating implementations and proofs from given formal specification (Zhao et al., 2026; Bursuc et al., 2026).

sections.title: 7 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We presented AUXSPEC, framework for training models to generate program specifications in Lean with execution-based feedback. AUXSPEC pairs each declarative postcondition with an executable postcondition, and the postcondition equivalence theorem states that both agree on all valid inputs. This allows us to evaluate specifications by directly executing test cases, without proving each case separately. At the same time, we retain the declarative postcondition for formal correctness proofs. With this format, we synthesize and release 3,037 LeetCode problems, each with proved postcondition equivalence theorem. The dataset includes AUXSPEC-Test, held-out benchmark of 300 expert-reviewed problems, all with proved correctness theorems.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Training on the synthesized data with an execution-based reinforcement-learning reward yields 9B and 27B models, and the 27B model surpasses all frontier models on AUXSPEC-Test and outperforms all baselines in SpecGen pass@1 on the out-of-domain Verina benchmark. Since the models are trained only on synthesized problems, the gains on Verina suggest that training with the reward improves faithfulness to the problem description beyond the test cases used in the reward. We discuss the limitations of this work in Appendix J.

sections.title: AI USE STATEMENT
sections.content: We used generative AI tools to synthesize the dataset and to produce proofs. The pipeline uses LLMs to synthesize, repair, judge and rewrite specifications and implementations (Section 3, Appendices and K), and proof agents built on LLMs produce the postcondition equivalence and correctness proofs, which the Lean kernel checks (Appendix H). We did not use generative AI tools to develop the conceptual framework or to interpret results, and translation and qualitative data analysis do not apply to this work. We also used generative AI tools to edit the text, create figures, search the literature and format references. We reviewed all AI-assisted work, ran the AI-generated code, checked every number against the script that computed it and every citation against the original publication, and take responsibility for the final content of this work, including text, claims or artifacts produced with the aid of generative AI.

sections.title: ETHICS STATEMENT
sections.content: One of the authors carried out the expert review of AUXSPEC-Test, and 2 of the authors reviewed the accepted outputs (Appendix I), and the work involves no other human participants and no personal data. The problems come from LeetCodeDataset (Xia et al., 2025) and TACO (Li et al., 2023), both released under the Apache-2.0 license, with the web-crawled problem statements of TACO under CC BY 4.0. We use them for research with attribution and will release our data and models under compatible licenses. The released models generate specifications and implementations for programming problems, and every accepted implementation remains checkable by proof against the postcondition.

sections.content: C.1 SOURCE SELECTION The LeetCode problems combine 2,869 problems of LeetCodeDataset (Xia et al., 2025) with 746 free problems collected from the site after the dataset snapshot. Of the 746 problems, 263 pass buildability filter that requires at least 3 examples and Python function signature and excludes database, shell, concurrency and design problems. The seeds are 3,109 problems, 2,864 from LeetCodeDataset and 245 from the site. We take the Codeforces and AtCoder problems from the train split of TACO (Li et al., 2023). For RL, we add problems from the train and test splits of TACO, including Aizu, CodeChef and GeeksforGeeks problems, and 989 Codeforces problems from openr1/codeforces (Penedo et al., 2025). Problems are admitted with at least 3 tests, reference solution, and single accepted answer, since one reference output cannot label problem with several accepted answers. Stored tests whose inputs violate the constraints of the problem description are removed before use, which drops 1,028 of 90,885 test rows on Codeforces and 2,119 of 22,115 on AtCoder. Difficulty in Table 3 follows the labels of LeetCode and TACO and the ratings of openr1/codeforces. The 1,484 problems without label, including all Aizu problems, take the tier that an LLM judge assigns in the conversion audit, where easy problems need direct simulation or single formula, medium problems standard technique and hard problems non-obvious idea or combination of techniques. C.2 PROBLEM FORMAT Each Codeforces and AtCoder problem, whose input is given from standard input, is rephrased into typed function interface and admitted only when the reference solution still passes the stored tests through that interface. Conversion admits 3,490 of the 4,314 Codeforces problems (80.9%). The rejected problems have stored tests that no reference solution reproduces (361), inputs that change under parsing and unparsing (259), several accepted answers (184), or other harness errors (20). Freezing the test cases removes 205 more problems, 201 of which lack 3 invalid inputs for L1b, and leaves 3,285. Of the 1,440 AtCoder problems, conversion admits 892, an audit for descriptions that drop stated condition and for examples that violate the stated constraints leaves 677, and freezing leaves 623. Most AtCoder rejections at conversion are inputs that change under parsing and unparsing (352 of 548), which trace to faulty stored tests such as leading zeros or counts that do not match the input.

sections.title: D EVALUATION
sections.content: D.1 METRICS Compile@k and Pass@k. We follow the standard definition of pass@k (Chen et al., 2021) and define compile@k by analogy. For problem with samples, compile@k is 1 when at least one sample compiles, and pass@k is 1 when at least one sample meets the acceptance criteria of Section 2. The reported value is the mean over problems, which equals the unbiased estimator of pass@k (Chen et al., 2021) since exactly samples are drawn per problem. Test case alignment compares the test lines of sample with the frozen test cases regardless of layer headings, and Lean code blocks are extracted regardless of the capitalization of the language tag. D.2 TOKEN EFFICIENCY We measure output tokens per response and per solved sample  (Table 14)  . AUXSPEC-27B-RL requires the fewest output tokens per solved sample of all 13 models in the 4 generation settings. On SpecGen of AUXSPEC-Test, it requires 80% fewer tokens per solved sample than GPT-5.6-Sol, the most economical frontier model (2.7K vs. 13.2K), while its pass@1 is 35.9 points higher (65.7% vs. 29.8%; Table 4). RL lowers the cost per solved SpecGen sample at both model sizes, as pass@1 grows faster than the response length (19.3K to 2.7K tokens for the 27B model and 36.0K to 11.0K for the 9B model). RL changes the length of the reasoning trace in opposite directions at the 2 model sizes. Reasoning traces of the 27B model become shorter after RL, whereas reasoning traces of the 9B model become longer (1.6K to 0.4K and 1.7K to 4.6K thinking tokens per SpecGen response). plausible reading is that the larger model needs less explicit reasoning to state specification, whereas the smaller model relies on longer reasoning to reach correct output. An early supervised fine-tuning run of Qwen3.5-9B compiles 5.05% of the 1,208 SpecGen samples and 3.8% of all 3,596 samples on the held-out problems. Classifying the first compiler error of the failed samples shows that 40.8% misuse Mathlib declarations, through application type mismatches (17.3%), invalid fields or projections (14.7%) and type mismatches (8.7%), and 65.2% once unknown identifiers (11.6%) and missing instances (12.8%) are counted. With retrieved declaration names in 58% of the answers, the failures come from the use of Mathlib. Corpus. Synthesis augments prompts with Mathlib declarations retrieved for the problem (Appendix G.1.2), and across the 3,109 LeetCode problems the retrievals cover 1,381 distinct declarations, of which 1,298 are found in the pinned Mathlib source. These declarations come from 411 files, and we take all declarations of those files rather than the retrieved ones alone, which yields 26,936 declaration heads. The heads are rewritten with DeepSeek-V4-Flash (DeepSeek-AI, 2026) into English lessons that state the content, the application, the occasion and the contrast of declaration, which follows the rewriting of raw corpora into reading-comprehension text (Cheng et al., 2024) and textbook-style synthetic corpora (Gunasekar et al., 2023). On-policy distillation trains student models on self-generated responses with token-level supervision from teacher models (Agarwal et al., 2024). sections.content: Attribution. We attribute the SpecGen drop to estimator bias, which lowers entropy throughout training, to mode collapse, which moves probability onto form that often fails to compile, and to teacher redundancy, which makes the teacher term uninformative about sample success. 1. Estimator bias. With k3 inside the advantage, the policy gradient is biased estimate of the reverse KL gradient that also raises the forward KL, and this configuration is reported to collapse training (Shah et al., 2026). The entropy decline of Figure 9 matches this bias. 2. Mode collapse. The pipeline sets the decidable form as the first executable postcondition and replaces the form through instance synthesis or separate definition when compilation fails (Section 3.1), and the form covers 35.5% of synthesized problems as result. Evaluation scores single samples without compiler feedback. We conjecture that the mode-seeking reverse KL (Agarwal et al., 2024; Jin et al., 2026) moves probability onto this frequent form, including on problems where the form does not compile. The student adopts the form in 54.6% of samples on problems where the teacher never adopts it. OPD therefore amplifies the form beyond teacher usage. 3. Teacher redundancy. Teacher models with higher scores help only when offering capabilities beyond the experience of the student (Li et al., 2026a). Teacher and student are fine-tuned on the same data, and although OPD within RL adds the fine-grained reward of reinforcement learning, the teacher term stays uninformative about which samples succeed. Identical tokenizers and chat templates rule out format mismatch, and on problems the teacher fails, the student stops at the failing stage of the teacher no more often after OPD than before.

G.1 PREPROCESSING G.1.1 TEST CASES For each of 3,109 problems (719 easy, 1,622 medium, 768 hard), we screen the stored examples and propose negative test cases, invalid inputs and incorrect outputs beside the positive test cases. Invalid inputs are proposed by category (a value just outside stated bound, size outside the stated range, container of the wrong shape, broken structural invariant, parameters invalid only together, value outside the stated domain), and incorrect outputs by category (a near miss, suboptimal feasible answer, an unattainable answer, the answer under relaxed constraint, an output of the wrong shape, degenerate answer). Benchmarks store negative test cases beside positive ones (Ye et al., 2026a;b), since specification that accepts correct outputs on the given examples can still accept incorrect outputs (Endres et al., 2024). proposed incorrect output is admitted when the reference solution, run on the proposed valid input, returns an output that is not reordering of the proposed output. Invalid inputs are proposed together with the violated constraint and are dropped on coinciding with valid example of the problem. For the test cases, we store the provenance (public example or synthesized) and the admission round. test case judged wrong is replaced by held-back test case at most once per problem. Analysis. sections.content: instances from the compiler diagnostics for up to 3 rounds. When the supplied instances still fail to elaborate, separate definition is generated. Only separate definition can disagree with the postcondition, which the L2a and L2b test cases detect on the tested outputs and the postcondition equivalence theorem excludes on all valid inputs. Appendix G.5 reports the counts by form. Judges. The postcondition judge is given the problem description, the constraints, and the postcondition source. rejection quotes sentence of the description and names an output that the postcondition admits and the problem excludes. The executable postcondition judge is given the constraints, the accepted precondition and postcondition, and the executable postcondition, and rejection names valid input with witness or counterexample that the executable postcondition misses or wrongly admits. The tautology judge rejects postcondition that computes the output. Problems whose natural statement is the transformation itself are labeled in advance by majority vote of 3 classifier calls, and the label exempts the problem from the tautology judge. The rejected component is repaired with the named error, or replanned for an error in the plan. G.2.1 EXAMPLE PROBLEMS Separate executable postcondition. We illustrate the format with problem 1955 Count Number of Special Subsequences from AUXSPEC-Test (Figures 13 and 14). In this problem, we are given an array over {0, 1, 2} and need to count, modulo 109 + 7, the subsequences of the form 0a1b2c with a, b, 1. The postcondition states the result as the size of the set of index sets whose selected elements take this form. The executable postcondition enumerates all subsets of the indices, bruteforce computation that finishes on the short test inputs. The implementation counts in 1 pass with 3 counters, for subsequences of 0s, of 0s followed by 1s, and of 0s, 1s and 2s, since an element either extends or skips the subsequences counted so far. Since neither specification mentions the counters, the correctness theorem relates the recurrence to the set of index sets. For this problem, natural postcondition characterizes the valid index sets as exactly those that select subsequence of the form 0+1+2+ from the input. This characterization is not directly executable, since it ranges over arbitrary finite sets of natural numbers. However, every relevant index set is contained in the input indices. The executable postcondition therefore enumerates 2{0,...,input.length1} and counts the subsets satisfying the same property. The two formulations describe the same relation but are not definitionally identical in Lean, so the postcondition equivalence theorem connects the logical characterization with the bounded enumeration. Executable postcondition through type class resolution. We illustrate the decidable form with problem 523 Continuous Subarray Sum from AUXSPEC-Test (Figures 15a, 15b and 16). In this problem, we are given an array of non-negative integers and positive integer and need to decide whether some contiguous subarray of length at least 2 sums to multiple of k. The postcondition states that the result is true exactly when there exist 2 indices and an integer multiplier such that the subarray between the indices sums to k. The executable postcondition applies decide to the postcondition, which compiles only when type class resolution finds Decidable instance for the unfolded proposition. The existential over natural-number indices and an integer multiplier has no such instance as stated, since the quantifiers range over unbounded domains. The pipeline therefore synthesizes type class instance that bounds both indices by the length of the array, replaces the multiplier by integer divisibility, and proves the bounded proposition equivalent to the original with decidable of iff. Type class resolution then assembles the executable postcondition from this instance and the library instances for bounded quantifiers and divisibility, so the executable postcondition agrees with the postcondition by construction (Appendix H.2). The implementation, omitted from the figure, scans prefix sums modulo with map from each remainder to the earliest prefix index at which the remainder occurs, and the correctness theorem relates this scan to the existential of the postcondition.

sections.title: IMPLEMENTATION
sections.content: Implementation planning is given the accepted specification as read-only text and selects an algorithm with cost argument, listing specification definitions to call and definitions to replace with reason. The plan is checked before generation for termination argument based on decreasing quantity of the input, stated cost consistent with the approach and the input bounds, replacement justified by cost or by different question, and an algorithm that computes the answer, without search over candidates. Beyond the properties in Section 3.1, the implementation judge reports computations already available in the specification.

sections.content: G.3.1 ANALYSIS Test cases on small inputs admit false positives (Li et al., 2022), and the implementation judge rejects 717 of the 3,667 implementations (19.6%) that pass all test cases (Figure 18). Fuel parameters (270). The implementation recurses on fuel argument, which hides nontermination on inputs beyond the test cases. Cost beyond the input bounds (234). The implementation is correct but exceeds the cost that the stated input bounds allow, known as slow positive (Li et al., 2022). Restated executable postconditions (198). sections.content: H.1 METHOD We prove the postcondition equivalence theorems with decompose-and-prove loop, which is widely adopted strategy for formal proofs (Jiang et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024; Ren et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026b), run by main agent and set of subagents (Figure 23).

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Figure 23. The decompose-and-prove loop. Solid edges carry the named objects, and the dashed edge returns an open goal to decomposition. The main agent holds the queue of problems and hands problem to one subagent, together with the form of the executable postcondition and the proofs of the closest problems already proved. The subagent compares the postcondition and the executable postcondition and produces proof sketch (Jiang et al., 2023), which records the structure common to both postconditions and states one lemma for each remaining clause. The lemmas are given sorry bodies and the file is compiled once, which checks that the lemmas close the theorem before any lemma is proved (Li et al., 2026b). decomposition that fails is restated by the same subagent, since the next decomposition is built from the open goal. The subagent then proves the lemmas one at time against the compiler, and each proof is verified against the frozen statement with SafeVerify (GasStationManager, 2024), bumped to Lean 4.32, which checks that no declaration of the problem was changed and that the theorem depends on the standard axioms only. H.2 POSTCONDITION EQUIVALENCE THEOREM We analyze the proofs by the form of the executable postcondition (Appendix G.2), since the form fixes the statement of the theorem. Executable postconditions that evaluate the postcondition through decidability instance agree with the postcondition by construction. Separate definitions replace quantifier of the postcondition by computation, and the postcondition equivalence proof shows that the replacement loses nothing on valid inputs. The computation is an enumeration that stands in for set, reformulation that decides different property, or bound that stands in for an unbounded quantifier. Plausible samples valid inputs and checks that the executable postcondition accepts the output of the reference implementation. counterexample is correct output that the specification rejects. 2. Validity. Plausible samples inputs and checks that the validity predicate agrees with the reference validity predicate. counterexample is an input that one predicate admits and the other rejects. We apply the specification-side rubric of Table 41. Expert review confirms 90 of the 100 accepted outputs, 43 of AUXSPEC-27B-RL and 47 of AUXSPEC-9B-RL  (Table 44)  . The 2 reviewers find 7 and 5 errors in their 60 problems and agree on all 20 shared problems, including the same 2 errors. Each error comes with concrete input that the validity predicate admits outside the constraints, which makes the verdict checkable rather than judgment. All declarative and executable postconditions are correct, and all 10 errors were found in the validity predicate. The missing constraints are guarantees that the answer fits in 32-bit integer (3 problems), value ranges and alphabets (3), structural guarantees on the input (3) and time format (1). The postconditions of these outputs therefore remain faithful on every input that the constraints admit. The tests against the reference miss these errors, since random inputs rarely reach the boundary of missing constraint. We acknowledge that the expert review covers only 100 outputs which is small sample, yet the errors found converge to the same kind. The models produce correct postconditions but are highly likely to miss boundary conditions of the constraints in the validity predicate. One possible reason is that the acceptance criteria offer little guidance on the validity predicate, since the specification quality judge assigns clauses that restrict the input to the validity predicate without checking them (Appendix K.3) and only the test layers L1 and L1b check the validity predicate on few inputs  (Table 7)  . Checking the validity predicate against the stated constraints is direction for future work (Appendix J). Table 44. sections.title: J LIMITATIONS
sections.content: Despite the contributions of AUXSPEC to specification generation in Lean, the work has several limitations that we hope to address in future work. Repair at inference. The repair tasks train the models on failed rollouts and are evaluated for single round  (Table 4)  , and the same tasks support self-refinement loop at inference, where the model repairs an output on compiler messages and test results over several rounds (Ye et al., 2026b). Pass rates over rounds would show how much of the gap to frontier models such loop closes. Scope of expert review. single reviewer covers the 300 AUXSPEC-Test problems and finds errors in 21 of them, including 9 specification errors in problems with proved postcondition equivalence theorem (Appendix I.1), and 2 reviewers review 100 accepted SpecGen outputs of the RL models (Appendix I.2). The training problems are checked by test cases, judges and postcondition equivalence proofs without review and need reviewed sample to estimate the error rate of the training data. Proofs for generated outputs. Generated specifications and implementations are accepted without proofs of the two theorems (Section 2). We prove the postcondition equivalence theorem afterwards for the accepted outputs of the RL models (Appendix H.4). proof shows only that the 2 postconditions agree. Whether the declarative postcondition and the validity predicate state the problem still rests on test cases, judges and expert review. Validity predicates. All errors found by the expert review of accepted outputs are input constraints missing from the validity predicate (Appendix I.2). The acceptance criteria check the validity predicate only with test cases. judge that compares the validity predicate with the stated constraints would cover this part in synthesis, training and evaluation.

sections.title: K PROMPTS
sections.content: The boxes below are condensed versions of the prompts, in the order of Figure 1. Every prompt has the same five parts in the order the model reads them, the role, the input, the task, the rules and the output format, and problem text is marked as untrusted data so that instructions inside problem statement are not followed. The boxes keep the rules that the analyses of Appendix refer to and drop the worked examples, the formatting rules and the injected library facts. The component names follow the paper. The prompts given to the models are in Appendix K.2, and the judges of Appendix K.3 run as the acceptance criteria of synthesis, in evaluation and in the reward. K.1 SYNTHESIS PIPELINE

sections.title: General planner
sections.content: ROLE Contract planner. Fixes everything about one problem that does not require specification thinking, before the specification side runs. INPUT problem (description, constraints, examples; untrusted), signature, default_lean_types, and on retry the ruling that found the previous plan incomplete. TASK Decide the Lean types, the interface names and the preconditions clauses, and record the domain facts. Everything fixed here is frozen; downstream roles follow it exactly. RULES 1. You own the representation: for every parameter and the output, declare the Lean type that is best for stating and proving this problem, weighing faithfulness, simplicity of the statements and the proof debt of the correctness proof. 2. Interface names describe what is computed, never how. 3. The preconditions clauses transcribe the stated constraints in the problems words: nothing dropped, nothing invented, no operational re-encoding. Where the input encodes something, state the encodings well-formedness. 4. The implementation algorithm is not yours to fix; later stage plans it once the specification exists. OUTPUT One JSON object: input_spec, lean_types (with rationale), interface, v_plan, domain_facts.

sections.title: Postcondition planner
sections.content: ROLE Specification planner. Receives the frozen types and precondition plan, and shapes the postcondition on top of them. INPUT problem (untrusted), lean_types, v_plan, negative_aims (what each frozen negative test targets), and on retry the previous ruling. TASK Plan the vocabulary and the shape of the postcondition in prose, no Lean. The postcondition states what correct output is; it does not produce one. Two statements are required: whether result is the kind of object that could be the answer, and what distinguishes the correct one from the others of that kind. RULES 1. State whether the second statement concerns the object the first exhibits or every object of that kind; universal reduced to the exhibited object is no bound. 2. result occurs inside relations that constrain it, never as the left side of an equation whose right side computes it. The test: conceal the right side and ask whether correct result remains distinguishable. 3. Keep out every operation that answers in the degenerate case instead of having no answer there (Set.ncard on an infinite set, sInf on the empty set, truncated subtraction, xs[i]!); it makes different specification, not false one. 4. Computability is not consideration; quantifiers range over the problems natural domain, and stated bound is hypothesis inside the quantifier, never truncated range. OUTPUT One JSON object: the two statements, second_statement_ranges_over, vocabulary, witnesses.

sections.title: Postcondition formalizer
sections.content: ROLE Specification formalizer. Renders the plans two prose statements as the specification side of one problem. INPUT plan (names and types binding), problem (untrusted), sketch_preview (the final file with your sections as holes), verified_library (declarations compiled against this toolchain), frozen_cases (layer, frozen input and output, and the expression the plan fixed). TASK Write the specification helpers, the precondition, the postcondition and the L1 and L1b guard commands. Theorem statements and module structure are machine-written; the test rows are frozen, and you write each row as one guard command. RULES 1. Decidability is not your concern; bounding or enumerating quantifier to make it computable is defect. 2. Specify the what, never the how: IsLeast result over result = sInf S. Mirroring an algorithms structure is defect. 3. The precondition is total Bool function covering exactly the stated constraints; the postcondition returns Prop and says the plans two sentences and nothing further. library declaration whose definition is what you were about to write is that same proposition, with the librarys lemmas. 4. The frozen rows are contract: one guard command per row, none for row that is not there, values preserved exactly. OUTPUT design note, then one Lean fence with Representation (only when needed), Specification helpers, the precondition, the postcondition and Unit tests.

sections.title: Test form judge
sections.content: ROLE Judge of whether guard command states the frozen test row it was written for, called when the mechanical comparison could not settle it. INPUT The frozen rows (test_id, layer, input and output as frozen JSON, the expression the plan fixed) and the guard command written for each. TASK Two mechanical checks ran first: the shape check (right layer, right anchor, right polarity) and the expression check (verbatim, then token by token). Rule on the rows where the tokens differ. RULES 1. The frozen JSON is the authority, not the plans expression. 2. Count when counting decides it: replicate, range, map over range. 3. Two expressions are equivalent when they elaborate to the same term; notation, grouping and redundant ascription do not change the test. missing or extra parameter or value that differs anywhere is different test. 4. Judge the denotation, not the style. When the evidence does not settle it, answer false and say what you could not determine. OUTPUT One JSON object with ruling per row: equivalent (true or false) and reason.

sections.title: Executable postcondition router
sections.content: ROLE Route analyst for the executable postcondition of one problem. Decides how it will be organized before anyone writes it. INPUT problem (untrusted), frozen_spec, test_inputs (with the length of every list and string), plan (whose domain_facts often supply the bounding fact). TASK The executable postcondition restates the frozen postcondition as Bool that compiled evaluation can run on the frozen inputs. The difficulty is cost: mirroring the quantifiers directly can be exponential in the input. Choose one of three routes: reshape (restate what is quantified over so the count collapses), truncate (bound quantifier by fact the problem supplies) or enumerate (range over finite encoding of the candidates). RULES 1. bounding_fact is the one fact the cost argument rests on, stated so reader could check it against the problem. 2. The executable postcondition is judge, never solver: it quantifies over candidates or verifies the answers defining property. shape that computes the answer by its own algorithm and compares is refused downstream, whatever its cost. 3. Name the route hasty writer would reach for and the cost that rules it out at these input sizes. OUTPUT One JSON object: route, bounding_fact, shape (in prose), rejected.

sections.title: Executable postcondition formalizer
sections.content: ROLE Writes the executable postcondition for frozen postcondition, following the route decided for it. INPUT plan, frozen_spec (read-only target), sketch_preview, route_plan, decidability_trial_error (why the decidable form was not available), verified_library, frozen_cases. TASK Write one Lean section with the executable postcondition and its helpers, and the L2 and L2b guard commands. Record the route taken and the fact that bounds it in note before the fence. RULES 1. total Bool function named base_name + _check, with the specifications argument order. 2. Bridge toward the frozen postcondition, never toward weaker reading of it; mirror its clause structure so the equivalence theorem is provable clause by clause. 3. Every recursion or fold must already be present in the postconditions own definitions: the equivalence proof should need only unfolding and structural alignment, never an algorithmic insight. Never compute the answer by another method and compare it with result. 4. Bound every quantifier to structure derived from the input. Size is measured, not hypothetical: what settles an enumeration is running it. 5. The fast algorithm belongs to the implementation; an evaluation that finishes belongs here. OUTPUT design note, then one Lean fence with the executable postcondition section and Unit tests.

sections.title: Implementation planner
sections.content: ROLE Implementation planner. The postcondition and the executable postcondition are accepted, and the algorithm is planned against them rather than against the problem statement alone. INPUT problem (untrusted), plan (impl_name binding), frozen_spec, frozen_executable_postcondition (read-only), verified_library, frozen_cases, and on retry the judges ruling. TASK Decide how the answer is computed and at what cost. This is the only section where running time is judged: the guards run the algorithm on the frozen inputs, so an exponential approach fails by timeout. Say which accepted definitions the algorithm calls and which it replaces, with the cost difference. RULES 1. approach names the standard efficient algorithm, not the first one that terminates; cost states its running time in terms of the input. 2. frozen definition is passed over on one of two grounds, and the entry says which: too slow (both figures given) or different structure required (the finer definition named). An entry on neither ground is rewrite that should have been call. 3. termination names the quantity the recursion consumes; Nat carried along so the recursion has something to count down is not such quantity. 4. The algorithm computes the answer; the specification says what correct answer is. Do not evaluate the specification over candidates and return the one that satisfies it. OUTPUT One JSON object: approach, cost, calls, replaces, termination. Root-cause analyzer ROLE Root-cause analyst, called only when local repair cannot proceed: symptom recurred after repair, repairer declared the fault lies elsewhere, or an error cannot be placed by line. INPUT error_report, sections (each labelled frozen or repairable), assembled_source (the whole file with line numbers), harness_regions, frozen_tests, history (the repair attempts so far), plans. TASK Rule which block is at fault, so the pipeline repairs the true target instead of the symptoms location. plan may also be ruled faulty, which triggers one replan. RULES 1. Rule on evidence in the diagnostics and sections, never on which line happened to error; symptom location and fault location are different things. 2. frozen test literal is ground truth by default. Rule it wrong only on evidence you can quote: the case does not violate the constraint its own rationale cites, or documented answer contradicts the problems own examples. 3. Prefer the cheapest sufficient target: section over plan, plan over declaring the run dead. 4. When the specification itself contradicts the tests, the run fails rather than the specification being weakened. OUTPUT One JSON object: fault (section with its title, plan, or frozen), reasoning (the decisive evidence), confidence.

sections.title: Specification repairer
sections.content: ROLE Specification repairer. Repairs exactly one broken section; everything else is frozen. INPUT broken_section, diagnostics (message, line, source line), context_sections (read-only), plan, attempt_history (what earlier rounds tried and how each ended), verdict (the ruling naming the target). TASK Read the diagnostics, fix the target section and return it. The reply replaces that section byte-for-byte; no other bytes of the file change. RULES 1. Minimal change: fix the diagnosed fault and keep the rest of the section byte-identical where possible. The plans names are frozen. 2. If the only repair that compiles would weaken the specifications meaning, return the section unchanged and mark it no-faithful-repair. 3. Two technical-looking repairs count as weakening: narrowing quantifiers domain to bound the problem does not state, and replacing quantified clause with Bool computation that decides it. 4. If the true fault lies in read-only section, return the body unchanged and mark it fault-elsewhere with the section named. OUTPUT Exactly one section with the targets title, followed by one line attempt: <one sentence>.

sections.title: Negative test case proposers
sections.content: INVALID INPUTS (L1b) Role: adversarial proposer for the validity layer. Input: problem (untrusted), signature, valid_examples, quota. Task: make the precondition hard to write. lenient predicate looks correct against valid inputs alone and stays wrong forever, so the measure of case is which wrong predicate it defeats: = 9 against 1 <= <= 8 defeats every predicate that forgot the ceiling. case no plausible wrong predicate would accept has raised the difficulty by nothing. When the examples do not show the range you need, ask instead of guessing. INCORRECT OUTPUTS (L2b) Role: adversarial proposer for the correctness layer. Input: problem (untrusted), signature, case (a valid input and its true output), aim (the flaw family to try first), quota. Task: make the postcondition hard to write. Name flaw weak postcondition could have (an optimization stated as achievable but never as best, count that misses case, search that forgets boundary), then write the wrong answer that flaw admits. wrong answer with no flaw behind it catches nothing. ADMISSIBILITY Task: keep frozen input only if compiled evaluation could check postcondition against it. The cost of an input is the number of candidates the postcondition ranges over, measured before the call for each standard shape, and about ten thousand is the ceiling. OUTPUT Each proposer returns JSON array of cases, each with the flaw or constraint it targets; the admissibility judge returns keep or refuse with reason. K.2 MODEL PROMPTS The models receive one of the 4 system prompts below, condensed. The user turn gives the problem, the constraints and the test cases, and for CodeGen the given specification. repair turn repeats the original user turn and adds the current file and the review of each failed stage. Without test cases in the prompt, as in Table 5, the SpecGen and CodeGen prompts replace the given test cases by test cases derived from the statement.

sections.title: SpecGen
sections.content: TASK Formalize the algorithmic problem in Lean 4 as validity predicate, an ideal specification and an executable checker, and check the predicate and the checker on the given test cases with guards. RULES 1. State the specification with the definitions of the statement, so that it characterizes the correct result instead of computing it. Quantify over the objects the statement defines, and bound quantifier only by bound the statement states. An optimum is attained by feasible candidate and is no worse than every feasible candidate, decision holds exactly when witness exists, and count is the size of the set of objects with the stated property. Use result = input only for formula the statement gives or for sequence of steps it prescribes. 2. Define the validity predicate to accept exactly the inputs that satisfy the stated constraints. 3. Define the checker to decide the specification on valid input, with each quantifier bounded by range the input determines: decide of the specification with registered instances where every quantifier is bounded, hand-written Bool function otherwise. 4. Complete each definition without sorry, and use none of admit, native_decide, noncomputable, partial, unsafe and Classical. OUTPUT One Lean file: import Mathlib, docstring restating the problem, then Specification helpers, Validity predicate, Ideal specification, Decidable specification (with <name>_check_iff_spec left as sorry) and Unit tests with guards under layers L1, L1b, L2 and L2b.

sections.title: CodeGen
sections.content: TASK Implement the algorithmic problem in Lean 4 against the given specification, with correct output for each input the constraints allow, and check the implementation on the given test cases with guards. RULES 1. Prove termination of each recursive definition by structural recursion or termination_by measure. 2. Choose an algorithm within log factor of the best known method, so that the implementation finishes on the largest allowed input. 3. Complete each definition computably and without sorry, with the constructs banned for SpecGen. OUTPUT One Lean file with Input, Output and the representation types copied from the given specification, then Specification helpers, Implementation helpers, Main algorithm and Unit tests with guards under layer L3. SpecGen-Repair TASK Repair the Lean 4 specification so that the file compiles, all guards evaluate to true and the specification states the problem faithfully. RULES 1. Locate the fault before editing, starting with the first compiler error. 2. Make the smallest change that removes the cause, and keep the names and argument order of isValidInput, <name>_spec, <name>_check and <name>_check_iff_spec. 3. State the specification declaratively where the problem allows; use result = input only where the statement prescribes the output. 4. Keep the checker clause-by-clause mirror of the specification with bounded quantifiers. 5. Complete each definition computably and without sorry. OUTPUT The complete repaired file, keeping the section headings and order of the current version.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: CodeGen-Repair TASK Repair the Lean 4 implementation so that the file compiles, all guards evaluate to true and the implementation returns correct output for each input the constraints allow. RULES 1. Find the cause before editing; termination error usually needs new measure or decreasing_by proof. 2. Apply the smallest edit that removes the cause, and keep the name and argument order of the main algorithm. 3. Prove termination as in CodeGen, and use an algorithm within log factor of the best known method. 4. Complete each definition computably and without sorry. OUTPUT The complete repaired file, with the section headings and order of the current version. K.3 EVALUATION JUDGES The judges below run as the acceptance criteria of synthesis, in evaluation and in the overall quality, test case alignment and non-tautology stages of the reward.

sections.title: Test case alignment
sections.content: ROLE Checker of the guard commands of file against the test rows the author was given. INPUT test_block (the given rows), guards (every guard of the file), unmatched (what mechanical check found where it could not match). TASK Decide whether the guards test exactly the given rows. RULES 1. Compare values only. Function names and spellings such as tuples, parentheses, arrays or string literals change nothing; changed, added, removed or reordered element is different value. 2. positive row is accepted, and an invalid input or wrong output is rejected with !. specification file tests positive row on both the validity predicate and the checker. 3. Guards beyond the given rows do not affect the verdict. OUTPUT problems (each missing, extra, changed or reversed, with the fix) and verdict, PASS or FAIL. Specification quality (SpecGen) ROLE Reader of specification against the problem it was written for. INPUT description (untrusted), constraints, specification. TASK Decide whether the specification accepts exactly the answers the problem accepts on valid inputs: soundness (it carries every condition on the answer) and completeness (it rejects no correct answer). RULES 1. Take the statement clause by clause. clause that constrains the answer must appear, clause that restricts the input belongs to the validity predicate, and resource bound stays out of the report. 2. Judge the Lean definitions by what they compute, evaluating each helper on small input. 3. Every finding names concrete values: for soundness, the quoted clause and value the specification admits and the problem rejects; for completeness, valid input, its correct output and the part of the specification that rejects it. OUTPUT missing_conditions and rejected_answers, each empty when there is nothing to report.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Checker quality (SpecGen) ROLE Reader of the executable checker. The guards pass, so on the frozen inputs it agrees with the specification. INPUT constraints, specification, checker. TASK Decide whether the checker accepts exactly what the specification does on every valid input. RULES 1. checker truncates where the specification quantifies over an unbounded domain. bound that is too small misses an object the specification admits; one that reaches objects the specification rejects can accept wrong output. 2. Report disagreement only with an object: valid input, its correct output by the statement, and the witness or counterexample one side reaches and the other does not. OUTPUT truncates, agrees_with_the_specification (YES or NO) and escapes, each with its direction, input, correct output and object. Implementation quality (CodeGen) ROLE Reader of the implementation. The guards pass, so it is correct on the tested inputs. INPUT constraints, specification, checker, implementation. TASK Judge what the tests cannot see: termination, cost, answers written back for the tested inputs and duplicated work. RULES 1. Report fuel parameter, and whether bound the recursion stops on can run out on an admitted input. 2. Mark the implementation too slow only when the best known method is faster by more than logarithmic factor and the implementation takes more than about 10^7 steps on the largest admitted input. 3. Report an implementation that branches on particular inputs to return particular answers. OUTPUT termination, cost (with too_slow), reproduces_tests, rewrote_the_checker and short reason. Non-tautology ROLE Lean 4 formalization auditor of the specification side. INPUT description (untrusted), constraints, specification. TASK Judge how much of solution the specification contains. RULES 1. DECLARATIVE: the condition on result is the condition of the statement, quantified over the objects of the statement. 2. ENUMERATIVE: the condition of the statement, but over list of candidates the specification builds itself. 3. TAUTOLOGICAL: the specification computes result by solving the problem, through recurrence, table, greedy rule or simulation the statement does not prescribe. 4. For ENUMERATIVE and TAUTOLOGICAL, describe the declarative specification in at most three sentences. OUTPUT reasoning, better_specification and verdict.
